We are a small team building forensic tooling that has to hold up under adversarial pressure every day. We are looking for engineers and researchers across computer vision, audio, ML infrastructure, and fraud who want to work where synthetic media meets real consequences.
Whether you want to run a pilot on your own media, integrate detection into a product, or explore a deeper partnership, tell us what you are working on and someone from the team will reply directly.

Plurall AI, spelled with two l's, is a New York company founded in 2024 that builds deepfake detection, fraud defense and proof-of-humanhood verification for trust, safety, security and compliance teams. Our models read forensic signals across image, video, audio and identity and return a verdict with the evidence behind it, so a reviewer can act on it rather than guess.

Plurall AI operates as a mathematics-first, post-AI cybersecurity threat detection company: evidence functions are chosen because a theorem forces the gap they measure, verdicts come from a decision rule whose optimality is proved, and every probability is calibrated and measured by slice.

Until recently, synthetic media sat in a gap between fraud law, privacy law and platform policy. That gap is closing. The rules below are the ones most likely to touch a trust, safety or compliance team in the next year. Dates are as enacted; this is a summary of public law, not legal advice.

What it asks of a platform: the 48-hour clock starts on notice, not on detection, so the practical burden is a reliable intake path and a way to find copies of the same media once one has been reported.

The AI Act's transparency obligations in Article 50 apply from 2 August 2026. Content that is a deepfake must be disclosed as artificially generated or manipulated, and providers of generative systems must mark their output in a machine-readable way. Generative systems already on the market have until 2 December 2026 to meet the marking requirement; the deepfake disclosure duty was not extended.

What it asks of a tool: labelling falls on the system that generates the content, which means detection systems should treat a missing label as unknown rather than as evidence of authenticity. Content made with tools outside the EU, or stripped of its marking, will carry no label at all.
What this means in practice
Labelling duties land on the tools that generate content; removal duties land on the platforms that host it. Neither lands on the person being impersonated.
A label is a useful signal and an unreliable one. The absence of a label proves nothing.
